TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Junub applies to male or female, singular or plural, describing a person in janaba. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (الزجاج): Al-Zajjāj notes that junub has the same form for one man, two men, and a group, as raḍī does. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa reads the junub traveler passing through as a traveler without water, who performs dry ablution and prays. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The forms تجنبتم, أجنبتم, and جنبتم all convey becoming junub; junub is generally indeclinable for gender, number, and plurality as a verbal noun-like form, though variants exist. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Some Arabic usage pluralizes junub as أجناب, like عنق/أعناق and طنب/أطناب; those who use جانب for the singular say جناب in the plural, like راكب/ركاب. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أحمد وإسحاق): Aḥmad and Isḥāq allow a junub to sit in the mosque after performing ablution, according to Ibn al-Mundhir. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أصحاب الرأي): The adherents of raʾy allow a traveling junub to perform tayammum, enter a mosque to draw water from its spring, and leave with it. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الثوري وإسحاق بن راهويه): Al-Thawrī and Isḥāq ibn Rāhwayh say a junub may cross a mosque only when necessary, after performing tayammum. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عطاء بن يسار): ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār reports that some Companions who became junub performed ablution, then came to the mosque and conversed there. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): Junuban coordinates with the circumstantial clause “while you are intoxicated”; janub applies to all genders and numbers like a verbal noun. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): Junub has the same form for singular and plural and for masculine and feminine because it functions like the verbal noun ijnāb. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhsharī says junub has one form for singular and plural and for masculine and feminine, like the verbal noun ijnaab; Abū Ḥayyān calls it fluent, Qurʾānic usage and notes plural forms جنبون، أجناب and dual جنبان. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (أحمد وإسحاق): Aḥmad and Isḥāq allow a junub who has performed ablution to sit in the mosque. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (علي): A second interpretation attributed to Ali takes the exception to mean a traveler who becomes junub and lacks water may perform prayer until water is available; reports from Ibn Abbas in one version, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and others say likewise. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أبو حنيفة ومالك والشافعي): Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafi‘i hold that a junub person may not remain in a mosque until bathing, or performing tayammum if water is unavailable or unusable. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أحمد): Ahmad permits a junub person to remain in the mosque after performing wudu. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عطاء بن يسار): Ataa ibn Yasar saw Companions sitting in the mosque while junub after performing prayer wudu; Ibn Kathir calls this report sound on Muslim’s criteria. BURHAN, d. 794 (author): Singular forms also occur in descriptions of groups, including junub, ẓahīr, najiyy, and the generic singular al-ṭifl. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (مجاهد): Mujahid says a junub person or menstruant may not pass through a mosque; the verse instead permits the traveler who lacks water to perform tayammum and pray. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says a person with smallpox, wounds, or ulcers who becomes junub and fears dying from bathing may perform tayammum. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Junub denotes a person in janaba after emission; it can be used as a singular noun or a plural.
